One-line judgment: chefs and head cooks are not about cooking one good dish yourself; they hold a kitchen's output, hygiene, cost and people together at the same time — directing and possibly taking part in preparing, seasoning and cooking foods such as salads, soups, fish, meats, vegetables and desserts, planning menus and setting prices and ordering and checking in ingredients, analysing recipes and pricing dishes by food, labour and overhead costs, determining how dishes are presented and creating decorative garnishes, arranging production schedules and staffing so meals go out on time, supervising the execution of hygiene rules and checking whether ingredients, finished dishes, equipment and work areas meet standards, instructing and training cooks and other kitchen staff, and recording production and operating data and arranging equipment purchase and repair. O*NET lists this occupation in the SVP range 6.0 to below 7.0, with an interest code of ERC (Enterprising, Realistic, Conventional), and the occupation page marks Bright Outlook. The core boundary is that there is no personal chef licence valid across both China and the United States; the U.S. FDA Food Code is a model code for jurisdictions to adopt, and the responsibility of the permit holder and the person in charge depends on local adoption and the institution's appointment; in Chinese mainland, the food business licence is obtained by the operating entity; the principal person in charge of the enterprise is fully responsible, and food safety management and directly responsible personnel must also perform their duties in accordance with the law and bear corresponding responsibility; the operating entity must appoint food safety management personnel as required. This page does not treat an industry average wage as the median for this occupation, nor does it present a skills certificate as automatic practice authorization.

Signals to keep exploring: you can watch several output lines at once under heat, noise and time pressure, and are willing to implement hygiene, allergen, temperature and retained-sample requirements item by item (the O*NET work context shows 88% face time pressure every day, 92% work indoors in a controlled environment every day, 87% have face-to-face discussions every day, 75% face minor burn and cut risks every day, 74% make decisions every day, 67% stand continuously or almost continuously and continuously handle and control objects and tools by hand, 65% are exposed to distracting or uncomfortable noise every day and 57% are exposed to extremely hot or cold temperatures every day), you are willing to stop and escalate on the spot when ingredients fail, hygiene is below standard or staff do not follow the rules, and you are willing to write the menu costs, output records, training and rectification records clearly and hand them over.

Conditions for pausing high investment first: you have not yet completed a full closed-loop exercise that runs from menu design and cost accounting, ordering and checking in ingredients, output flow and staffing, hygiene and allergen control, to output review and records; or you are unwilling to implement hygiene, temperature, allergen and retained-sample requirements item by item, unwilling to stop work when ingredients, equipment or hygiene are below standard, unwilling to mentor and correct other people's work; and do not treat having cooked a few dishes at home as proof that you already have kitchen organisation, cost control and food safety management ability.

Education, qualifications and authorization must be checked separately: O*NET lists this occupation in the SVP range 6.0 to below 7.0, and the education survey shows 54% of respondents think an associate's or other two-year degree is needed, 17% think a postsecondary education certificate is needed and 13% think a high school diploma or equivalent is needed; the occupation page lists 22 certifications (including Certified Executive Chef and Certified Working Pastry Chef from the American Culinary Federation, Certified Culinary Professional and Certified Culinary Professional Level II-III from the Foodservice Institute, and the AMSA Culinary Meat Selection & Cookery Certification from the American Meat Science Association), and lists 2 position titles approved by the U.S. Department of Labor for registered apprenticeship (Chief, Cook and Cook, Chief). There is no personal chef licence valid across both China and the United States: the U.S. FDA Food Code 2026 is a model code for jurisdictions to adopt, and the responsibility of the permit holder and the person in charge depends on local adoption and the institution's appointment, and it cannot be assumed that every chef is automatically the statutory person in charge; in Chinese mainland, the food business licence is obtained by the operating entity; the principal person in charge of the enterprise is fully responsible, and food safety management and directly responsible personnel must also perform their duties in accordance with the law and bear corresponding responsibility, and food safety management personnel are appointed by position. Education and training, industry certification, statutory qualification and work eligibility, job hiring and authorization, and the appointment of a food safety person in charge and the boundaries of charging and promising are five different things.

The focus of the position is kitchen output, hygiene, menu costs, purchasing and mentoring; the outputs include standard recipes, production schedules, receiving and inventory ledgers, inspection rectification and training records. Chefs may also take part in budgeting, purchasing and business decisions, with the scope depending on job authorization. U.S. wages are occupational statistics, while the Chinese accommodation and food service average is only an industry proxy.

The work of this occupation can be divided into three categories: first, kitchen operations and output organisation (supervising and coordinating cooks and staff, explaining and demonstrating preparation, cooking and plating, determining production schedules and staffing needs, checking the quality of raw and cooked foods, and preparing and cooking food for special occasions); second, menus, costs and purchasing (analysing recipes and pricing menu items by food, labour and overhead costs, estimating quantities and costs, ordering and requisitioning and checking in quantities and quality, negotiating prices with sales representatives, discussing banquet and special occasion menus with customers, and coordinating budgets and purchasing); third, hygiene, compliance, people and records (supervising the execution of hygiene rules, checking whether supplies, equipment and work areas meet standards, recruiting and training and demonstrating new techniques, recording production or operating data, and arranging equipment purchase and repair). All three share one chain built around stable output, traceable hygiene, verifiable costs and teachable staff.
Kitchen operations and output organisation

Check the covers, reservations and banquet demand for the service → determine the production schedule and staffing and station assignments → organise preparation and cooking to the standard recipes and output standards → check the quality and temperature of ingredients, part-prepared items and finished dishes → determine the presentation and complete the decorative garnish → re-check the order and timing of service and handle rework and replacements
Menus, costs and purchasing

Analyse recipes and account for food, labour and overhead costs → price menu items and re-check the gross margin → estimate quantities and costs and order and requisition as needed → check in quantities and quality and handle non-conforming items → negotiate prices and payment terms with sales representatives → build inventory, loss and count records and re-check them periodically

Rotas and training → check temperature and time, cross-contamination and applicable retained samples to the applicable rules → check work areas and equipment → record rectification and re-check; when anomalies are found, control the relevant ingredients or equipment first and report, and potential accident risks are handled under the statutory duty to suspend operations and report, and cannot simply wait for additional position approval.

Chefs and head cooks centre on kitchen output, hygiene, cost and people management; food service managers specialise in store operations, budgets, personnel and compliance management, first-line supervisors of food preparation and serving workers in the rotas and supervision of front-line food preparation and serving staff, restaurant cooks and institution and cafeteria cooks and fast food cooks in preparing and cooking to standard, and dietetic technicians in the preparation and supervision of dietary nutrition and therapeutic diets. Similar names or being in the same kitchen does not mean that licensing and food safety responsibility, pricing and purchasing decision authority and people management authority can be exchanged.
Core purpose

Make every meal stand up at the same time on stable output, controllable hygiene, verifiable cost and staff meeting standards: use standard recipes and output standards so taste and portion are consistent, use temperature, time and cross-contamination control and records so food safety is traceable, use cost accounting and inventory and loss records so pricing and gross margin can be verified, and use rotas, training and rectification so staff work to standard.
Main objects and basis

The objects are ingredients, part-prepared items and finished dishes, standard recipes and output standards and plating styles, kitchen equipment and refrigeration, freezing, holding and cooking facilities, tableware, packaging and cleaning and sanitising supplies, and menu, price, cost and inventory data; the people you work with include kitchen staff at all stations and service staff, purchasing, warehousing and suppliers, store operations and finance positions, customers and banquet hosts, and regulators and inspectors. The basis is the standard recipes and output standards and menu cost data, the hygiene requirements and temperature and time control requirements for food purchasing, receiving, storage, processing and service, the allergen, cross-contamination and applicable food retained-sample and cleaning and sanitising requirements, the hygiene, operating training and health management requirements for the position, and the statutory requirements and institutional rules for the food business licence and the appointment of food safety management personnel and consumer rights protection.
Core process

Rotas and division of work, ordering and receiving, ingredient pre-processing and preparation, cooking and seasoning to standard, output checks and plating, hygiene and temperature and allergen control, cost and inventory checking, training and correction, and records, rectification and handover.
Main outputs

Menu, cost and pricing records, ordering, receiving and non-conforming item handling records, standard recipes and output standards and plating notes, hygiene and temperature and cross-contamination and applicable retained-sample inspection and rectification records, rota, training and assessment records, production plans and service records, inventory, loss and count records, and equipment purchase and repair records.
Responsible party

Kitchen output, hygiene, cost, purchasing and people responsibilities are divided by position and institutional authorization. In China the principal person in charge of a food production and operation enterprise is fully responsible for food safety, and food safety management personnel perform their duties by position; if a head cook bears direct management responsibility or commits unlawful acts they may also bear responsibility in accordance with the law, and cannot be exempted on the ground of not having been appointed the statutory person in charge. Interfaces for facilities, suppliers and employment matters must be made clear, and when anomalies occur the relevant ingredients or equipment must be withdrawn from use first and reported.
Access and licensing

The food service business licence is obtained by the entity according to the business items; the principal person in charge, food safety management and directly responsible personnel perform their duties in accordance with the law, and a head cook's purchasing, personnel and external commitments are subject to the position's division of work. FDA2026 is a model code for jurisdictions to adopt: 2-101.11 provides for the permit holder to be or to designate the PIC and to ensure that person is present during operation, including multi-department and regulator-recognised low-risk exceptions; 2-102.12 covers the PIC food protection manager certification and low-risk exceptions. In practice this is checked against the locally adopted version, and not every chef holds the same certificate. Articles 3/5/6/7/17/20—21 of China's 2025 Provisions on the Primary Responsibility of Enterprises: the principal person in charge is fully responsible and must appoint food safety officers as required, with certain enterprises also appointing a director; the director and food safety officer must have management ability and complete training and assessment, with at least 40 hours of training per year. Where a potential accident risk is found, a veto recommendation to stop the relevant activity must be raised, and the enterprise must immediately suspend operations and report to the county-level market regulation department where it is located; direct liability is determined in accordance with the law and is not excluded because no appointment was made or no additional approval was obtained. Collective catering units have separate rules, and the enterprise provisions are not applied wholesale to all canteens.
Boundary of the conclusion

The output, hygiene and cost records describe how the kitchen ran for that shift or that meal within the given menu, ingredients, equipment and authorization; they are not the same as a determination of food safety responsibility and legal liability, nor do they replace the determinations that the operating entity and the regulator make under the licence and the rules, and they are updated as menus, ingredients, staff and equipment change; when cited, the menu version, ingredient batches and sources, equipment condition and record period should also be stated.

Before starting work, check at least six items: the job duties (whether they lean toward output and back-of-house management, menu development and cost, banquets and large events, multiple stores or a central kitchen, or purchasing and warehousing), whether you carry duties related to appointment as food safety management personnel and the licence, the working-time form (regular shift, split shift, night shift or holiday peaks) and rest arrangements, people management authority (recruiting, rotas, assessment and dismissal) and budget approval authority, who is responsible for equipment and premises conditions and investment and refurbishment, and the pay method (fixed salary, or salary plus bonus or profit share) and assessment indicators.
Occupational framing

U.S. O*NET-SOC35-1011.00, Job Zone3/SVP6 to less than 7, Bright Outlook, interest ERC (69/64/56). The 2025 industry distribution is accommodation and food services 72% and other 28%, which is not industry wages. The U.S. definition is to direct and possibly take part in food preparation and cooking, menu pricing, ordering and records. The 2022 Chinese classification code text includes Chinese cuisine cooks 4-03-02-01 (PDF physical page 207), covering dish cost and selling price accounting, kitchen management and banquets; Western cuisine cooks 4-03-02-03 cover menu development. The duties overlap with U.S. 35-1011.00, but the cooking style and the scope of coordination differ, and no one-to-one mapping was established this round; the absence of a mapping must not be described as the related occupation not existing in China.
Education and training path

In the United States O*NET gives Job Zone 3 (medium preparation) and SVP 6.0 to less than 7.0. The education survey asks what education new employees need: 54% answered an associate's or other two-year degree, 17% a postsecondary education certificate and 13% a high school diploma or equivalent; this is not the share of incumbents' education. BLS Table 1.2 lists the typical entry-level education as a high school diploma or equivalent with related experience of five years or more; the statistical purposes differ. The certification entry lists 22 items and the summary lists 2 registered apprenticeship position titles, and conditions must be checked with the issuing body or programme in each case. In China, food safety management personnel must complete training and assessment under the applicable rules; people who come into contact with directly consumed food must obtain an annual health examination and a health certificate before starting work.
Methods and tools

O*NET lists 14 software skill categories; Hot Technologies separately lists 7: Excel 7%, Outlook 6%, Office 5%, Word and PowerPoint 4% each, Google Sheets below 1%, and the Facebook share unavailable. The denominator is Lightcast 2025 unique U.S. job postings linked to this occupation, not an incumbent or institutional adoption rate. On-site tools include stoves, thermometers, weighing equipment, refrigeration equipment and inventory cost systems, trained according to the institution's configuration, and recruitment word frequency alone cannot be used to infer specific equipment or AI adoption.
Safety and work permits

The work is mainly indoor kitchen work under heat and noise and standing. The O*NET work context shows: 92% work indoors in a controlled environment every day; 88% face time pressure every day; 88% wear common protective or safety equipment every day; 87% have face-to-face discussions every day; 75% face minor burn, cut, bite or sting risks every day; 74% make decisions every day; 71% have telephone conversations every day; 67% stand continuously or almost continuously and continuously handle and control objects and tools by hand; 65% are exposed to distracting or uncomfortable noise every day; 63% are in contact with others continuously; 58% perform repetitive motions continuously; 57% are exposed to extremely hot or cold temperatures every day; 50% consider working with a work group extremely important. The work must follow institutional hygiene and safety procedures and equipment instructions, taking care over burn and cut protection for knives, cutting equipment, hot oil, steam and open flames, and complying with the cleaning and sanitising, waste disposal and pest control requirements for food processing areas.
Training and regulatory requirements

Chinese food service licensing is checked against Articles 4/10—12 of Order No. 78 for the entity, items, premises and facilities; exceptions such as pre-packaged sales only are checked separately, and small food service follows local rules. Health and job training are checked against Articles 44—45 of the Food Safety Law and Article 14 of the operating standard. FDA2026 is a model code for jurisdictions to adopt: 2-101.11 provides for the permit holder to be or to designate the PIC and to ensure that person is present during operation, including multi-department and regulator-recognised low-risk exceptions; 2-102.12 covers the PIC food protection manager certification and low-risk exceptions. In practice this is checked against the locally adopted version, and not every chef holds the same certificate. Section 7.9.1 of China's 2018 operating standard requires retained samples for school canteens (including nurseries), elderly care and medical canteens, central kitchens and collective meal distribution units; it also applies to construction site canteens serving more than 100 people and to collective dining for more than 100 people or catering for major events. Other food service providers are assessed according to the recipients, quantity, variety, control capability and the relevant provisions, and it cannot be stated uniformly that all kitchens require it. Where it applies, retained samples are stored in dedicated airtight containers by variety in dedicated refrigeration equipment for at least 48 hours, with at least 125g per variety sufficient for testing, and identified and recorded by a designated person (7.9.2—4).
Pay and working hours

Insufficient evidence: no precise occupational wage distribution or one-to-one occupational mapping for Chinese chefs and head cooks was obtained this round. Working hours centre on the kitchen floor and meal peaks; in the O*NET questionnaire 79% answered more than 40 hours per week, which is not a contractual hours guarantee. Wages use BLS2025 OEWS, with the national page showing a median of 30.03 USD/hour and 62,470 USD/year. The employment projection comes separately from BLS Table 1.2: 220.3 thousand in 2025, 234.7 thousand in 2035, up 6.6%, and 25.2 thousand openings per year on average. The 2025 Chinese accommodation and food service figures of 62,461 CNY for non-private units and 55,123 CNY/year for private units are only an industry average proxy and cannot be used as a quote for head cooks. Before starting work, check hours, rest, bonuses and purchasing and pricing authority.

Chefs and head cooks (O*NET-SOC 35-1011.00, Chefs and Head Cooks) direct and may take part in the preparation, seasoning and cooking of foods such as salads, soups, fish, meats, vegetables and desserts; they may plan menus and prices, place orders for purchasing, and keep records and accounts. Daily work includes: supervising the execution of hygiene rules to ensure staff comply with standards and regulations; explaining the preparation, cooking, garnishing and presentation of food to cooks or other staff; supervising or coordinating the work of cooks and staff engaged in food preparation; ordering or requisitioning food and other supplies to maintain operating efficiency; checking whether supplies, equipment and work areas meet established standards; checking the quantity and quality of products received; checking whether the quality of raw or cooked food meets standards; estimating the quantities and costs of needed supplies such as food and ingredients; coordinating the plans, budgets and purchasing of all food service operations within the institution; analysing recipes and pricing menu items by food, labour and overhead costs; planning and directing or supervising food preparation and cooking activities across multiple kitchens or restaurants; determining how food is presented and creating decorative garnishes; preparing and cooking a variety of foods routinely or for special guests and events; determining production schedules and staffing needs to ensure meals are served on time; meeting customers to discuss menus for special occasions such as weddings and banquets; recruiting and hiring cooks and other kitchen staff; recording production or operating data on designated forms; meeting sales representatives to negotiate prices or order supplies; arranging equipment purchase or repair; demonstrating new cooking techniques or equipment to staff; and collaborating with others to plan and develop recipes or menus taking account of factors such as seasonal availability of ingredients or expected customer numbers. It carries responsibility for output quality, hygiene, cost and people management, but does not replace the determination of food business licensing, food safety responsibility and penalties by the operating entity and the regulator.

O*NET occupational identity and tasks: O*NET-SOC 35-1011.00 Chefs and Head Cooks, page updated in 2026, SVP range 6.0 to below 7.0, and the occupation page marks Bright Outlook. The official duties are 'Direct and may participate in the preparation, seasoning, and cooking of salads, soups, fish, meats, vegetables, desserts, or other foods. May plan and price menu items, order supplies, and keep records and accounts.'; the page lists 21 tasks (all core tasks), covering supervising the execution of hygiene rules to ensure staff comply with standards and regulations (97), explaining the preparation, cooking, garnishing and presentation of food to cooks or other staff (89), supervising or coordinating cooks and staff engaged in food preparation (88), ordering or requisitioning food and other supplies to maintain efficiency (86), checking whether supplies, equipment and work areas meet established standards (83), checking the quantity and quality of products received (83), checking whether the quality of raw or cooked food meets standards (82), estimating the quantities and costs of needed supplies (82), coordinating the plans, budgets and purchasing of all food service operations within the institution (76), analysing recipes and pricing menu items by food, labour and overhead costs (75), planning and directing or supervising preparation and cooking activities across multiple kitchens or restaurants (72), determining how food is presented and creating decorative garnishes (71), preparing and cooking a variety of foods routinely or for special guests and events (71), determining production schedules and staffing needs to ensure meals are served on time (71), meeting customers to discuss menus for special occasions such as weddings and banquets (66), recruiting and hiring cooks and other kitchen staff (65), recording production or operating data on designated forms (64), meeting sales representatives to negotiate prices or order supplies (64), arranging equipment purchase or repair (63), demonstrating new cooking techniques or equipment to staff (62), and collaborating with others to plan and develop recipes or menus taking account of factors such as seasonal availability of ingredients or expected customer numbers (61).

U.S. wages (BLS May 2025 OEWS framing, as shown on this occupation page): the hourly median is 30.03 USD and the annual median is 62,470 USD; the hourly 10th, 25th, 75th and 90th percentiles are 18.22, 23.29, 37.86 and 47.39 USD, and the annual 10th, 25th, 75th and 90th percentiles are 37,900, 48,440, 78,750 and 98,560 USD. The median means half of workers earn above and half below that value; it is not entry-level pay or a starting-pay promise; these wage percentiles describe wage and salary positions and do not represent the business income or profit of self-employed chefs or food service owners.

No Chinese occupational wage distribution or one-to-one occupational mapping corresponding precisely to 35-1011.00 was obtained this round. National Bureau of Statistics 2025 average annual wages for accommodation and food services are 62,461 CNY for non-private units and 55,123 CNY for private units, covering all positions in urban legal entities with 5 or more employees and excluding sole proprietors and freelancers. Both figures are industry proxies and cannot be used to infer head cook starting pay, median, monthly wage or business profit.

The current O*NET detail page marks Top industries2025: accommodation and food services 72%, and the remaining 28% on the industry page; BLS projects employment of 220.3 thousand in 2025, 234.7 thousand in 2035, a net increase of 14.4 thousand, growth of 6.6%, and 25.2 thousand openings per year on average, with the self-employed share at 6.8% in 2025. Bright Outlook does not guarantee individual employment; the OOH explanation of demand includes income growth and demand for eating out. Ingredient prices and labour costs are operating conditions suggested for editorial observation, not causal estimates from Table 1.2.

O*NET importance ratings: training 78, coordination 77, building teams 76; skills monitoring 75, speaking 72, critical thinking 69, listening 66, mathematics 50, science 19; knowledge food production 78, production and processing 76, customer service 73. These are ratings on a 0—100 scale, not respondent percentages. Interest ERC, with interest scores Enterprising 69, Realistic 64, Conventional 56; work style impact ratings dependability 88, leadership 86, attention to detail 83, stress tolerance 71. The 14 software categories and the Hot Technologies7 items are different lists and do not set a personal competence cut-off.

paragraphs: This page compares chefs and head cooks with six adjacent directions on the same set of dimensions: occupational direction, core work and outputs, key differences, and which direction each preference is better suited to. The adjacent directions are described according to their own official occupational descriptions and do not mean that position titles or licensing and food safety responsibility and pricing and personnel authority can be exchanged.

Evidence note: occupational directions and core outputs are based on O*NET-SOC 35-1011.00 and the official descriptions of the adjacent entries (U.S. framing); the adjacent occupations listed by this evidence route are food service managers, dietetic technicians, first-line supervisors of food preparation and serving workers, and fast food and institution and cafeteria cooks, while restaurant cooks are a same-chain direction among the O*NET related occupations; licensing and the appointment of the food safety person in charge, and pricing, purchasing and personnel authority must be verified separately under each jurisdiction and institution and contract (the U.S. FDA Food Code is adopted by jurisdictions, and the responsibility of the permit holder and the food safety person in charge depends on local adoption and the institution's appointment); this page does not present any direction as a shortcut to a career change.

The table below compares how chefs and head cooks and the adjacent directions differ in duties and outputs; the basis for judgment is the main outputs, the object of responsibility and the qualifications and authorization required, not how similar the position titles are.

Food service managers specialise in whole-store operations, budgets, personnel policy and licensing compliance; this occupation's scope of responsibility is kitchen output, hygiene, back-of-house cost and people, and pricing, purchasing and personnel policy must be executed under the authorization of the store and the operating entity.

If you would rather do store operations, budgets and personnel management, look first at food service managers; if you would rather manage kitchen output, hygiene and cost so that they are traceable, look first at this occupation.
Responsible for store operations, budgets, personnel and compliance management, with outputs centring on revenue, cost and customer satisfaction.
Food service managers

First-line supervisors mainly coordinate food preparation and service staff directly and may also order supplies, handle personnel matters and draft budgets; this occupation centres on kitchen cooking, menus and output organisation, and specific authority cannot be excluded on the basis of the title.

If you would rather coordinate preparation and service staff directly, compare first-line supervisors; if you would rather coordinate kitchen menus, output and mentoring, compare chefs; authority is checked position by position.
Supervising the rotas and work of front-line food preparation and service staff, with outputs centring on on-site efficiency and service standards.
First-line supervisors of food preparation and serving workers

Restaurant cooks mainly prepare and cook and may also supervise staff, purchase and plan and price menus. Chefs place more emphasis on kitchen organisation and mentoring; the two have overlapping tasks and should be compared by the actual position.
If you would rather prepare and cook day to day, compare restaurant cooks; if you would rather organise the kitchen team and menus, compare chefs.
Preparing and cooking dishes in a restaurant kitchen to the standard recipes and output requirements, with outputs centring on the quality of the dishes for each service.
Restaurant cooks

Institution and cafeteria cooks centre on high-volume catering for schools, hospitals and similar settings and may also plan menus, purchase and mentor. It cannot be inferred from the institutional setting alone that pressure is lower or menu flexibility smaller.

If you would rather do high-volume catering in institutions such as schools and hospitals, compare institution and cafeteria cooks; check the population served, schedule and authorization by position.
Providing meals in volume in institutions and cafeterias to fixed menus and nutrition and cost requirements, with outputs centring on volume consistency and cost control.
Institution and cafeteria cooks
Dietetic technicians assist with meal and nutrition plans under the supervision of a dietitian and may take part in nutrition assessment and meal planning; chefs centre on kitchen output operations.
If you are willing to assist with meal and nutrition plans under the supervision of a dietitian, compare dietetic technicians; if you would rather manage kitchen output, compare chefs.
Preparing and supervising meals to dietary and therapeutic diet requirements, with outputs centring on compliance with nutrition and therapeutic requirements.
Dietetic technicians

Fast food cooks mainly serve from a short, limited menu process and may also order supplies or coordinate schedules; chefs place more emphasis on kitchen organisation, menus and cost, and authority cannot be judged entirely from the title.
If you would rather serve quickly from a limited menu, compare fast food cooks; if you would rather coordinate menus and the kitchen team, compare chefs.
Preparing and serving quickly to a fixed process in a fast food setting, with outputs centring on service speed and standardisation.
Fast food cooks

Conclusion: the basis for choosing a direction is the main outputs, the object of responsibility and the qualifications and authorization required, not how similar the names are; once a direction is chosen, check item by item whether the target position carries duties related to appointment as food safety management personnel and the licence, the working-time form and rest arrangements, purchasing, pricing and people management authority, equipment and premises conditions and refurbishment responsibility, and the pay method and assessment indicators, and keep written confirmation.

The following five items are deployment and review suggestions that should be adjusted to the institution's control points and applicable rules; they are not a granted uniform five-step operating authorization.

First confirm the scope of matters you may decide and those you must escalate (menus, pricing, purchasing, personnel and licensing), the version of the menu, recipe and price data you rely on, and who monitors and reviews the critical control points.

Articles 3/5/6/7/17/20—21 of China's 2025 Provisions on the Primary Responsibility of Enterprises: the principal person in charge is fully responsible and must appoint food safety officers as required, with certain enterprises also appointing a director; the director and food safety officer must have management ability and complete training and assessment, with at least 40 hours of training per year. Where a potential accident risk is found, a veto recommendation to stop the relevant activity must be raised, and the enterprise must immediately suspend operations and report to the county-level market regulation department where it is located; direct liability is determined in accordance with the law and is not excluded because no appointment was made or no additional approval was obtained. State Administration for Market Regulation: Provisions on Food Production and Operation Enterprises Implementing the Primary Responsibility for Food Safety (2025 amendment)

paragraphs: Boundary: this section describes occupational risk and work responsibility boundaries, not an evaluation of individuals or institutions; specific procedures and handling processes are determined by the applicable jurisdiction, food law and local adoption, the institution's food safety management system and the authorization of the operating entity.

The main risks include failure of temperature and time and hygiene control, allergen cross-contact, knife and heat source injuries, mentoring errors, cost losses and misjudging the boundary of responsibility. Check control points, hygiene and equipment and exception handling to the applicable rules; the same protective configuration, all ingredient anomalies or appointment rules cannot be applied uniformly to every kitchen. Section 7.9.1 of China's 2018 operating standard requires retained samples for school canteens including nursery, elderly care and medical canteens, central kitchens and collective meal distribution units; it also applies to construction site canteens serving more than 100 people and to collective dining for more than 100 people or catering for major events. Other food service providers are assessed according to the recipients, quantity, variety, control capability and the relevant provisions, and it cannot be stated uniformly that all kitchens require it. Where it applies, retained samples are stored in dedicated airtight containers by variety in dedicated refrigeration equipment for more than 48 hours, with at least 125g per variety sufficient for testing, and identified and recorded by a designated person (7.9.2—4).

The sources separately support occupational tasks, group exposure conditions, Chinese operating standards and primary responsibility, the FDA model code and OSHA safety recommendations; the OSHA young worker kitchen guidance is used only for the corresponding heat source and handling controls, and adolescent accident data is not used to infer accident rates for head cooks. Specific labour contract disputes and local rules were not checked this round.
Chefs and head cooks themselves and all kitchen workers

Failure of temperature and time control or hygiene execution can cause foodborne illness. The O*NET importance rating for the hygiene supervision task is 97 and the time pressure questionnaire shows 88% answering every day, and neither can be used to infer accident probability or to assert that peaks are necessarily more dangerous.

Check temperature and time and equipment calibration, separation of raw and cooked, hand hygiene and exception handling against the applicable jurisdiction and food and process requirements; sections 7.1/7.4/7.7—9 and 14.4 of China's operating standard support the corresponding requirements, and the FDA Chapter 3 temperature and time conditions are checked separately, and the same threshold cannot be applied across jurisdictions. Section 7.9.1 of China's 2018 operating standard requires retained samples for school canteens including nursery, elderly care and medical canteens, central kitchens and collective meal distribution units; it also applies to construction site canteens serving more than 100 people and to collective dining for more than 100 people or catering for major events. Other food service providers are assessed according to the recipients, quantity, variety, control capability and the relevant provisions, and it cannot be stated uniformly that all kitchens require it. Where it applies, retained samples are stored in dedicated airtight containers by variety in dedicated refrigeration equipment for more than 48 hours, with at least 125g per variety sufficient for testing, and identified and recorded by a designated person (7.9.2—4).
Omitting temperature measurement and recording to speed up service, or continuing to use ingredients that are past time or below temperature.
Chefs and head cooks themselves and the menu and output step

Ingredient substitution, garnishing and reused utensils can cause allergen cross-contact. The complete recipe and supplier information should be checked, and the importance rating of 71 for the plating task cannot be used to infer respondent percentages or the step most prone to accidents.

First check the complete recipe and supplier information, and re-check allergens and cleaning controls after any change to the order. 3-602.12(C) of FDA2026 provides for written notification of major food allergens for unpackaged food, and the actual obligation is checked against local adoption; ordinary menus in China do not directly adopt this U.S. requirement. Dedicated utensils or areas, or validated cleaning and process, follow the specific control plan; when uncertain, pause the relevant catering and report, and do not treat customer consent as a food safety guarantee.

Changing a recipe without checking allergens, reusing utensils without effective cleaning, or not updating the service side; failing to provide written notification where locally required. Not every reuse of utensils or verbal communication is automatically unlawful.
Chefs and head cooks themselves and the equipment and knife work step

Knives, equipment, hot oil and steam can cause injuries; the O*NET75% answering that they are exposed daily to minor burn and cut hazards, 88% using common protection every day and 67% continuously using their hands describe exposure conditions rather than the daily injury rate.

Keep guards and knives in good order according to the equipment instructions; choose protection according to the specific cutting or heat source hazard, and cut-resistant gloves cannot serve as heat-resistant gloves. The OSHA guidance recommends heat-resistant gloves, non-slip shoes, standing to the side when opening steam ovens and avoiding opening under pressure; ask for help with heavy hot liquid pots. Wait for hot oil to cool before moving or filtering it for frying, and do not treat two people carrying hot oil as permission for safe practice; when equipment is abnormal, withdraw it from use and report for repair.
Carrying hot oil one-handed or moving quickly through crowded aisles, or removing equipment guards for convenience.
Chefs and head cooks themselves and the people management step

Insufficient mentoring and fatigued work can increase errors, and labour disputes are handled according to the actual employment terms. The ratings of 89 for the explaining task and 88 for supervising and coordinating are O*NET importance ratings; the 58% performing repetitive motions continuously is a work context response share, not an injury rate.

New staff complete position hygiene, operating and equipment safety training with records before starting work; rotas, rest and overtime arrangements are made clear and comply with institutional rules and employment regulations; work that does not follow the rules is corrected on the spot with records and follow-up; matters involving dismissal, rewards and penalties and labour disputes are handled under institutional authorization and process.
Letting untrained people operate cutting or cooking equipment independently, or substituting verbal scolding for proper training and records.
Chefs and head cooks themselves and the cost and purchasing step

Failure to check portions, yields, losses or expenses distorts pricing and gross margin. The O*NET ratings of 82 for estimating quantities, 75 for recipe pricing and 64 for supplier negotiation are all importance ratings, not respondent percentages.

Work to the standard recipes and portions and re-check yields; count inventory periodically and check losses and discrepancies between records and stock; calculate order quantities from actual sales and storage conditions and keep a safety stock; re-check food, labour and overhead costs and the gross margin before pricing; major purchases and price commitments follow institutional authorization and process.
Ordering by experience without counting inventory, or using ingredients that do not meet standards in order to keep costs down.
Chefs and head cooks themselves and the operating entity and regulatory handover step
Promising licensing and food safety responsibility beyond your authority or representing the unit externally creates legal and business liability that is hard to bear.

Chinese licensing is checked against the entity and the business items, and purchasing, personnel and external commitments follow the division of work by position; the principal person in charge, food safety management and directly responsible personnel perform their duties in accordance with the law and responsibility and penalties cannot all be pushed onto the entity. Articles 3/5/6/7/17/20—21 of China's 2025 Provisions on the Primary Responsibility of Enterprises: the principal person in charge is fully responsible and must appoint food safety officers as required, with certain enterprises also appointing a director; the director and food safety officer must have management ability and complete training and assessment, with at least 40 hours of training per year. Where a potential accident risk is found, a veto recommendation to stop the relevant activity must be raised, and the enterprise must immediately suspend operations and report to the county-level market regulation department where it is located; direct liability is determined in accordance with the law and is not excluded because no appointment was made or no additional approval was obtained. Collective catering units have separate rules, and the enterprise provisions are not applied wholesale to all canteens. FDA2026 is a model code for jurisdictions to adopt: 2-101.11 provides for the permit holder to be or to designate the PIC and to ensure that person is present during operation, including multi-department and regulator-recognised low-risk exceptions; 2-102.12 covers the PIC food protection manager certification and low-risk exceptions. In practice this is checked against the locally adopted version, and not every chef holds the same certificate.
Promising customers or staff that having a Chef at our store means all food safety requirements are met.

values: Fictional sample pack｜pen and paper or spreadsheets only, no cooking, no knives, no equipment operation, no food service.

A banquet for 20 people, 1 vegetable rice portion each. Each portion uses 0.08kg net rice (8 CNY/kg, 100% yield), 0.12kg net vegetables (10 CNY/kg, 80% net material rate) and 0.01kg oil (20 CNY/kg). No opening inventory and no safety stock; labour 20 CNY and overhead 16 CNY are fixed costs for the whole batch. The selling price is 12 CNY per portion, and the contribution rate for this question is (revenue − food − labour − overhead) / revenue.

Fictional work data: 2 people, each responsible for one station; A checks the order and receives goods for 10 minutes → weighs and preps ingredients for 20 minutes; B organizes utensils and the service sheet for 15 minutes; after both lines are ready, cooking takes 20 minutes → re-checking 10 minutes, sharing 1 piece of equipment; this is calculation only, not actual operation.

Exception injection: A's ingredient list states it contains peanuts while the customer order notes a peanut allergy; B's refrigeration reading contradicts another measurement and the historical time records are missing. Without on-site evidence it is forbidden to write a passing temperature or to release the meal; the applicable scope of retained samples is checked separately against the setting requirements.
Task｜submit the cost sheet, a two-option schedule, the exception record and the authorization check within 100 minutes.

Calculate the gross ingredients purchased for 20 portions, the cost of each ingredient, the total batch cost, the revenue and the contribution rate; then run a sensitivity calculation for a selling price changed to 10 CNY per portion.

Draw the 2-person parallel and 1-person serial options and calculate the critical path; list 3 self-check points. For each of the two exceptions, write the discovery, the object to pause, the evidence needed, the escalation recipient and the re-check conditions, and do not write unfounded compliance conclusions.
Reference solution｜cost, scheduling and exception loop.

Rice 1.6kg/12.8 CNY, vegetables 3kg/30 CNY gross, oil 0.2kg/4 CNY; food 46.8 CNY, total cost 82.8 CNY, revenue 240 CNY, balance 157.2 CNY, contribution rate as specified 65.5%; at a price of 10 CNY the revenue is 200 CNY, the balance is 117.2 CNY and the contribution rate is 58.6%. The contribution rate in this question includes labour and overhead and is not the same as the commonly used food gross margin in the industry.

Parallel preparation max(30,15)=30 minutes, plus cooking 20 and re-checking 10, giving 60 minutes in total; the 1-person serial option is 30+15+20+10=75 minutes. Overlapping use of equipment or omitting the re-check must not be treated as speeding up. Self-check: gross and net quantity units, the ingredient and allergen version, and the completeness of the re-check record.

For the peanut exception, pause the arrangement for that recipe and check the supplier's full label, alternatives and cross-contact controls, handing it to the authorized person to confirm; for the temperature exception, isolate the ingredients awaiting a decision, check the equipment, measurement and time records and report, and do not release on a single reading or an AI suggestion. The answer only verifies paper reasoning.
Usage boundaries｜the simulated data cannot be used for real food service or food safety judgments.

No real customer, employee or supplier data is used; do not actually cook, operate knives or heat sources, or try allergens. Passing the paper exercise does not equal mastering on-site work, nor does it grant a qualification, a food safety appointment or a pass in recruitment.
Piece one｜cost and pricing sheet

Attach the sample version, gross and net quantities, each cost item, the formulas, both the 12 CNY and 10 CNY options, the units and the differences from the reference solution; do not fill in real unit prices that are missing.
Piece two｜two-option schedule

Submit the station dependency diagram for the 2-person 60-minute and 1-person 75-minute options, the equipment constraint and three self-check points; ask the reviewer to check the formulas and the conditions before and after, and record the feedback; if there is no on-the-job reviewer, record clearly that it has not been reviewed.
Piece three｜exception and review record

List separately the peanut recipe conflict and the missing temperature and time evidence: the object to pause, the evidence list, the person submitting the report, the open items and the re-check conditions; all values are simulated and no actual measurement or compliance signature is written.
Piece four｜job authorization checklist

List education and experience, health management, food safety appointment, purchasing and pricing, personnel and budget, and working hours and pay separately; state the source and jurisdiction clearly and mark anything unclear as to be checked. The four pieces only prove how this exercise was handled and do not prove on-site competence.

values: Day 1｜boundaries and the position
Use O*NET and the current food safety rules to write the task, jurisdiction and authorization checklist; this whole week is paper-based and does not enter a real kitchen.
Day 2｜data verification
Organize the fictional 20-person menu, unit prices, net material rates, ingredient labels and two exceptions, check the units and record the version.
Day 3｜cost and pricing
Calculate the purchase quantities, the 82.8 CNY total cost and the contribution rates for the two prices, and record the formulas and the differences from the reference solution.
Day 4｜production scheduling
Draw the parallel 60-minute and serial 75-minute options and check the station dependencies and the non-overlapping use of equipment.
Day 5｜exception handling

Fill in the two records for the peanut conflict and the missing temperature and time evidence, explaining the pause, the reporting and the re-check conditions; do not invent on-site compliance evidence.
Day 6｜review feedback
Ask a reviewer to check the four pieces; if no on-the-job feedback is obtained, record it as not reviewed, and you can still self-check against the reference solution first.
Day 7｜investment decision

Organize the four pieces and the change records, and decide whether to continue, pause or compare an adjacent direction based on your interest in the tasks and the difficulty of completing them; the paper exercise does not test tolerance for heat or physical effort.

entries.answer: Directing and possibly taking part in the preparation, seasoning and cooking of foods such as salads, soups, fish, meats, vegetables and desserts, and possibly planning menus and prices, ordering supplies, and keeping records and accounts: supervising the execution of hygiene rules to ensure staff comply with standards and regulations; explaining the preparation, cooking, garnishing and presentation of food to cooks or other staff; supervising or coordinating the work of cooks and staff engaged in food preparation; ordering or requisitioning food and other supplies to maintain operating efficiency; checking whether supplies, equipment and work areas meet established standards; checking the quantity and quality of products received; checking whether the quality of raw or cooked food meets standards; estimating the quantities and costs of needed supplies; coordinating the plans, budgets and purchasing of all food service operations within the institution; analysing recipes and pricing menu items by food, labour and overhead costs; planning and directing or supervising food preparation and cooking activities across multiple kitchens or restaurants; determining how food is presented and creating decorative garnishes; preparing and cooking a variety of foods routinely or for special guests and events; determining production schedules and staffing needs to ensure meals are served on time; meeting customers to discuss menus for special occasions such as weddings and banquets; recruiting and hiring cooks and other kitchen staff; recording production or operating data on designated forms; meeting sales representatives to negotiate prices or order supplies; arranging equipment purchase or repair; demonstrating new cooking techniques or equipment to staff; and collaborating with others to plan and develop recipes or menus taking account of factors such as seasonal availability of ingredients or expected customer numbers.

entries.answer: The main risks include food safety incidents caused by failure to execute hygiene rules and improper temperature and time control, customer health risks caused by inadequate allergen labelling and cross-contamination control, cuts and burns from knives, cutting equipment, hot oil, steam and open flames, non-compliant work and labour disputes caused by inadequate mentoring and non-compliant employment, business losses caused by cost, loss and pricing deviations, and out-of-scope promises and legal risks caused by unclear boundaries of licensing and food safety responsibility; controls depend on confirming ingredients, equipment and premises conditions before work, item-by-item execution and recording of temperature, time, cross-contamination and retained samples at critical control points, working to procedure and using protection for knives, equipment and heat sources, closing the loop on training, correction and assessment, periodic checking of cost, inventory and losses, and a clear stop and escalation path.
entries.question: What risks should I pay attention to in advance in this job?

entries.answer: The fit signals are being able to keep output and hygiene stable under continuous service at peak times, being able to work out cost, loss and order quantities clearly, being able to stop work on the spot when ingredients, hygiene or equipment fall below standard, and being willing to mentor and correct others; the key is whether you have reviewable output and hygiene inspection records, cost and inventory and loss records and training and rectification records, rather than only having cooked a few dishes at home or a piece of kitchen experience.
entries.question: How do I judge whether this job suits me?

entries.answer: Menu cost and gross margin calculations, quantity and order quantity estimates, drafting rotas and production schedules, organizing inventory and loss ledgers, and organizing hygiene and temperature checklists and rectification ledgers can all be assisted; judging ingredient and output quality, executing and reviewing hygiene and critical control points, mentoring and correcting staff, and attributing food safety and cost responsibility are still checked and owned by authorized personnel.

entries.answer: The actual quality, temperature and freshness of ingredients on arrival, the actual differences in taste, mouthfeel, temperature and appearance of the output, whether critical control points are actually executed, the actual state of cross-contamination, allergens and retained samples, and whether rectification is effective and staff work to the rules must all be completed and documented by authorized or qualified people.

details: Articles 3/5/6/7/17/20—21 of China's 2025 Provisions on the Primary Responsibility of Enterprises: the principal person in charge is fully responsible and must appoint food safety officers as required, with certain enterprises also appointing a director; the director and food safety officer must have management ability and complete training and assessment, with at least 40 hours of training per year. Where a potential accident risk is found, a veto recommendation to stop the relevant activity must be raised, and the enterprise must immediately suspend operations and report to the county-level market regulation department where it is located; direct liability is determined in accordance with the law and is not excluded because no appointment was made or no additional approval was obtained. subject.summary: This page entry corresponds to chefs and head cooks (O*NET-SOC 35-1011.00, Chefs and Head Cooks): directing and possibly taking part in the preparation, seasoning and cooking of foods such as salads, soups, fish, meats, vegetables and desserts, and possibly planning menus and prices, ordering supplies, and keeping records and accounts — supervising the execution of hygiene rules, explaining preparation, cooking and presentation to staff, supervising or coordinating cooks and staff, ordering and requisitioning and checking quantities and quality to maintain efficiency, checking whether supplies, equipment and work areas meet standards, estimating quantities and costs and pricing menus by food, labour and overhead costs, determining production schedules and staffing needs, creating decorative garnishes, recruiting and mentoring and demonstrating new equipment and recording production and operating data; the work is mainly indoor kitchen work under heat, noise, standing and time pressure (92% work indoors in a controlled environment every day, 88% face time pressure every day, 75% face minor burn and cut risks every day, 67% stand continuously or almost continuously), and its duties do not replace the determination of the food business licence and food safety responsibility by the operating entity and the statutory responsible person; the occupation page marks Bright Outlook.
